daddu2026modular.summary: Presents a modular phased-array architecture for a 2 TW space solar power system from 400 identical stations.
daddu2026modular.abstract: A terawatt-class space solar power (SSP) infrastructure will require a scalable design that avoids the mass, assembly, and reliability limitations of monolithic orbital platforms. This paper presents a modular phased-array architecture in which a 2 TW space solar power system is built as a constellation of 400 identical 5 GW Space Solar Power Modules (SSPMs) operating in geostationary orbit. Each SSPM is a 4.3 km diameter filled circular aperture assembled from approximately 145,000 identical 10 m × 10 m Power Tiles. Each tile integrates thin-film triple-junction photovoltaics, solid-state 5.8 GHz microwave amplifiers, phase control electronics, and radiating antenna elements. The assembled SSPM functions as a coherent phased array capable of near-field focusing toward a dedicated terrestrial rectenna. A tailored amplitude taper and quadratic phase correction are used to generate an approximately flat microwave power-density profile over a ground receiving area while maintaining high beam-collection efficiency. The orbital dynamics of the low-areal-density structure are analysed with emphasis on solar radiation pressure, geopotential perturbations, gravity-gradient torque, and station-keeping requirements. A combined attitude and orbit control system using electric propulsion and control moment gyros is proposed to maintain beam-pointing accuracy, phase coherence, and constellation stability. pegetti2026brazil.summary: Examines Brazil's space legal framework against international approaches to find gaps for planetary defense and suggests legislative changes.
pegetti2026brazil.abstract: ABSTRACT The Brazilian legal framework for space operations is examined in this paper to find areas lacking planetary defense and to suggest legislative changes that could integrate Brazil into worldwide projects in this field. Brazilian legislation was investigated using a qualitative methodology based on documentary and comparative research, including the current Law No. 14,946/2024, in contrast to the regulatory frameworks of six major countries that have a planetary defense initiative in place. The study revealed important components such as formal acknowledgment of the threat, assignment of institutional responsibilities, and finance systems. The findings expose that Brazil has major legislative gaps that hinder the efficient development of national planetary defense capabilities, even though it has an established space program and pertinent scientific capability in astronomy. With a rising tendency toward integration between near-Earth object (NEO) monitoring programs and national civil defense systems, the comparative research reveals that all the space powers examined—except Brazil—have particular legal provisions for planetary defense. The study concludes that incorporating planetary defense into the Brazilian legal system would not only be a reaction to a growing issue but also a strategic chance for national scientific and technological advancement as well as for establishing Brazil as a proactive participant in world space governance.

ulambayar2026designing.summary: Examines the gap between Mongolia's Vision 2050 and sectoral policies to design resilient space governance for latecomer nations.
ulambayar2026designing.abstract: As the global space sector enters the NewSpace era, developing countries such as Mongolia face significant challenges in developing functional space programs without the institutional legacy of established space powers. This study examines the gap between Mongolia’s long-term development strategy, “Vision 2050”, its sectoral policy guidance for space science and technology, and the absence of a comprehensive national space governance system. Using Qualitative Systems Analysis (QSA), the study compares governance arrangements across advanced, developing, and emerging spacefaring nations. The method enables comparative evaluation of institutional interactions, regulatory adaptability, and governance structures in national space systems where quantitative indicators remain limited or difficult to standardize. The findings indicate that direct replication of traditional “Old Space” institutional models often produces structural misalignment in latecomer states with limited financial and technological capacity. In response, the study proposes an Agile Governance Model (AGM) based on the Governance–Resilience–Agility (GRA) Triad. The model combines strategic coordination, adaptive regulation, and operational implementation through a flexible governance structure emphasizing phased legal development, public–private partnerships, and national capacity-building. The study further argues that latecomer nations can avoid rigid legacy institutions by adopting modular governance structure

carvalho2026dual.summary: Dissertation on international humanitarian law for dual-use commercial satellites, focusing on Starlink use in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict.
carvalho2026dual.abstract: As modern warfare increasingly relies on objects and infrastructure that serve both civilian and military functions, a tension is created with the principle of distinction. This dissertation examines how International Humanitarian Law addresses dual-use objects, with particular focus on the use of Starlink satellites during the Russo-Ukrainian conflict. The use of Starlink satellites by Ukrainian armed forces highlights the legal uncertainty surrounding objects that support civilian life while providing concrete military advantages. The qualification of Starlink satellites as dual-use objects exposes the limits of the civilian/military dichotomy in Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I. The classification of satellite systems in this context necessarily raises questions about the applicability of International Humanitarian Law to outer space, as well as issues of state responsibility under the Outer Space Treaty and neutrality arising from the military use of privately owned space infrastructure.

szpak2026economic.summary: Compares economic threats in areas beyond national jurisdiction including outer space.
szpak2026economic.abstract: This article examines the growing economic threats associated with areas beyond national jurisdiction (ABNJ), including Antarctica, outer space, the high seas, and the deep seabed. Drawing on comparative analysis of legal instruments, scientific studies, and international reports, it identifies two overarching categories of risks: mature threats already visible in practice, such as monopolization, uncertain returns on frontier industries, IUU fishing, and piracy; and speculative threats arising from regulatory gaps, geopolitical competition, and technological inequalities. The study further distinguishes threats linked to resource exploitation from those resulting from ecosystem degradation, including climate impacts, tourism pressures, pollution, and orbital debris. It argues that fragmented governance and weak enforcement exacerbate these threats, creating systemic vulnerabilities that impact global economic stability. By offering the first comprehensive cross-domain typology of economic threats in the ABNJ, the article highlights the convergence of economic, environmental, and geopolitical pressures, underscoring the need for strengthened multilateral governance.

yazici2026situational.summary: Proposes a phased institutional pathway from space situational awareness to space traffic management, introducing a cooperative Orbital Stability Assessment and Index to measure coordination burden among operators.
yazici2026situational.abstract: Rapid growth in satellite deployments has transformed Earth orbit from a sparse operational environment into a continuously negotiated shared domain. Modern tracking networks increasingly detect conjunction risks, yet collision avoidance remains dependent on bilateral coordination between operators rather than predictable procedural rules. Space situational awareness (SSA) is therefore indispensable but incomplete: it provides probabilistic knowledge of orbital conditions but does not yet constitute a traffic management regime capable of ensuring consistent, system-level predictability. This paper examines how space traffic management (STM) can be developed by converting awareness into structured coordination through phased institutional design rather than immediate supranational authority. It distinguishes SSA from STM and identifies short-term improvements that establish interpretive interoperability without redistributing authority. To address scaling constraints, the paper introduces a cooperative Orbital Stability Assessment (OSA) producing a periodic Orbital Stability Index (OSI). As a pre-institutional diagnostic pilot involving civil safety service providers, commercial SSA analytics providers, and spacecraft operators, OSA would evaluate system-level coordination conditions by measuring coordination burden rather than incident occurrence, while OSI would synthesize those observations into a periodic assessment of whether coordination remains predictable and scalable

cao2026isru.summary: Reviews 15 years of ISRU and in situ fabrication and repair science and technology.
cao2026isru.abstract: In situ resource utilization (ISRU) and in situ fabrication and repair (ISFR) are critical research and technological paradigms for future space exploration. They aim to reduce reliance on Earth-supplied materials by utilizing resources available on celestial bodies, while enabling on-site fabrication and repair through the use and processing of local resources. ISRU and ISFR are strongly interconnected, with the shared objective of enabling more sustainable and autonomous long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. This work presents a comprehensive and critical review of scientific and patent literature published primarily between 2010 and 2025, complemented by selected earlier seminal contributions for context. The analysis provides an integrated perspective on major technological developments, key challenges, and emerging research directions in low-gravity and microgravity environments.

martinez2026space.summary: Questions whether space is a global common as international acceptance of the commons narrative declines.
martinez2026space.abstract: The notion of space as some sort of global common has been around since before the dawn of the Space Age and this notion has continued to be asserted by various commentators from time to time, most recently often in the context of space resource utilization. But, is space really a “global common” that “belongs” to all of humanity? This article discusses the concept of global commons as traditionally defined, understood, and applied on Earth. Then we review the evolution of commons-type language in multilateral documents and transpose the concept of the commons to the space domain, arguing that, while the freedom to engage in the activity of access and use outer space is a right held by all states under international space law, the domains of space themselves are not global commons or other such social constructs. Indeed, such constructs are mutable and not always correlated with peaceful, sustainable or prosperous uses of shared resources across history.

handelmazzetti2026jus.summary: Offers a normative assessment of force, limited force and hostile acts in space.
handelmazzetti2026jus.abstract: Abstract Outer space is an increasingly vital domain in military affairs. Satellites play a central role in modern military strategy: they act as sentinels for surveillance, facilitate secure communication and underpin strategic intelligence and precision operations. The importance of space systems is also reflected in the proliferation of various counter-space capabilities to disrupt, degrade or destroy space systems, either to protect one's own capabilities or counter the strategic advantage of adversaries. Hostile acts in space are not limited to kinetic action or missile-based attacks. In a world characterized by increasing geopolitical rivalry, competition often involves attempts to gain strategic advantage by using means and methods short-of-war. Hybrid warfare refers to the use of instruments and tactics of statecraft as a way of exercising power below the threshold of war—in the grey zone between war and peace—through kinetic (limited force or force-short-of-war) or non-kinetic hostile (‘soft war’) actions. This article aims to shed light on the strategic–normative dimensions of space security. We address the following central questions: How are various counter-space activities classified under international law? How should these activities be evaluated? And how can militaries respond to these activities? siddiqi2026modeling.summary: Develops a systems-theoretic model of how cumulative human activities affect the lunar environment.
siddiqi2026modeling.abstract: Abstract An increasing number of missions to the Moon are planned for the future. However, their long-term, cumulative impacts on the lunar environment are unknown. Research indicates that some important scientific discovery potential may be permanently lost, and exploration may become challenging due to effects of large-scale human activities. Motivated by these questions, we develop and present a generalizable systems-theoretic framework, called Sustainability Evaluations for Lunar Environment Exploration, for assessing the effects of human-built systems on the lunar environment. We contribute a scale and rate diagram of natural and anthropogenic processes on the Moon to provide comparative assessment of important processes that can dominate environmental effects and carry implications for human operations. Additionally, we derive metrics using functional-relationship diagrams of engineered systems to identify environmental effects based on exchange of matter, energy, and information. We demonstrate computation of two selected metrics: the area of the blast zone due to lunar landings and the trajectory of disturbed regolith mobilized from the lunar surface. For the cases considered, our results show that modern spacecraft (that may transport humans to the Moon) can have a landing blast zone area that would be 2–5 times larger as compared to the estimated landing blast zone area of the Apollo missions and up to 30 times larger as compared to some robotic missions. younger2026orbital.summary: Reviews orbital biomanufacturing supporting in-space logistics, manufacturing and resilience.
younger2026orbital.abstract: Space-based biomanufacturing has historically focused on long-duration crewed and exploration missions, but its greater potential lies in supporting in-space logistics, manufacturing, and servicing in Earth orbit. This article provides a strategic perspective on how shifting investments, policy, and R&D to orbital biomanufacturing could revolutionize defense, commercial, and civil sectors by enhancing supply chain resiliency, operational flexibility, ethical debris management, and commercial viability in Earth orbit.

saniotis2026prometheus.summary: Examines bioethics and environmental responsibility in outer space activities.
saniotis2026prometheus.abstract: It has only been since the 1960s that humans have possessed the technology to venture beyond the earth. Over the succeeding decades, our knowledge of space and how humans respond to its adverse conditions has significantly increased. To date, over 700 astronauts have entered space in countless space missions, a remarkable achievement given the severe space environment and its inherent dangers. Given the adverse nature of human activities since the advent of the Neolithic period (circa 10,000 BCE), which have been marked by significant biodiversity loss, terrestrial degradation, and periodic crises mainly due to maladaptive socio-political-ideological systems, will our current zeitgeist be transported to future non-terrestrial settlements? Otherwise, will our future descendants manage to develop new kinds of ethical systems which privilege communion with the cosmos? Consequently, this paper argues for the necessity of future space colonists to develop an “ethically based cosmic imperative” for thriving in extra-terrestrial habitats. I define this ethical cosmic imperative as a human need for creating ethical systems/ideologies in response to the unique environmental and social conditions space colonists will experience. nolan2026regolith.summary: Measures adhesion of lunar and Martian regolith simulants to PDMS and polycarbonate, finding substrate stiffness matters more than surface energy for dust adhesion in surface operations.
nolan2026regolith.abstract: ABSTRACT Dust adhesion is a critical challenge for lunar and Martian surface operations, causing equipment degradation, and reduced operational lifetimes. This study investigated the adhesion of three regolith simulants, Lunar Highlands Dust Simulant (LHS1D), Lunar Mare Simulant (LMS1), and Mars Global Simulant (MGS1), to polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and polycarbonate using two deposition methods: air deposition and rolling contact. Polycarbonate showed significantly lower area coverage than PDMS across all simulants and deposition methods ( p < 0.001). This was unexpected, as PDMS has lower surface energy, higher hydrophobicity, and higher roughness – properties typically associated with reduced adhesion. However, PDMS has a lower Young's modulus (3.2 MPa vs. 2.9 GPa), which may allow greater surface deformation and increased contact area. Experiments with a stiffer PDMS formulation (4.2 MPa) supported this, showing reduced adhesion with increased modulus. Rolling contact generally produced higher coverage than air deposition, and the finest simulant (LHS1D) showed the highest adhesion, consistent with increased van der Waals interactions for fine particles. Drying significantly increased adhesion on both materials. These findings suggest that substrate stiffness may play a more significant role than surface energy in controlling regolith adhesion, and that rigid, high‐modulus materials warrant further investigation for dust‐exposed surfaces in space environments.

karyda2026satellites.summary: Dissertation arguing Earth observation data can qualify as personal data under GDPR.
karyda2026satellites.abstract: This dissertation examines whether Earth Observation (EO) data collected by satellites can constitute personal data within the meaning of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It challenges the assumption that EO data fall outside the scope of data protection law and argues that their qualification as personal data requires a contextual, technology-sensitive assessment. The analysis is structured around the three elements of the GDPR definition of personal data, as developed by the Article 29 Working Party and confirmed by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU): "any information", "relating to", and "identification". The dissertation demonstrates that EO data satisfy the broad "any information" criterion regardless of their format or medium. It further argues that EO data may relate to natural persons through their content, purpose, or effects, particularly in applications such as geomarketing, geoscoring, smart-city initiatives, socio-economic analysis, risk assessment, and humanitarian operations. The decisive issue is identifiability. To assess this element, the dissertation develops the concept of the "3Ws of EO Data Processing"—by whom, for what purposes, and by which means—identification may occur. Drawing on CJEU jurisprudence, it argues that identifiability should be assessed through a relative approach. borshch2026use.summary: Analyses use of commercial space products and services for Ukraine's defence and security.
borshch2026use.abstract: The article analyzes the possibilities of using commercial space products and services in the interests of Ukraine’s national security and defense under the conditions of the full-scale armed aggression of the russian federation. It is shown that the provision of space-derived intelligence to Ukraine’s Defense Forces today rests on three components: partner assistance from NATO countries, commercial satellite products, and the development of national institutional capacity. The technical capabilities of modern commercial electro-optical and synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) satellite systems with a resolution of up to 1 m and finer are examined, along with the practice of integrating such data into the “Delta” information and communication system. Using the case of Ukraine's cooperation with ICEYE – from a crowdfunded contract in 2022 to an institutional agreement backed by the German government in 2024-2026 – the article illustrates the mechanism by which a one-off commercial product becomes a permanent element of defense infrastructure. A comparative analysis is conducted of partners’ institutional responses to the war’s “space lesson”: NATO’s pooled market-access model (the Alliance Persistent Surveillance from Space programme), the European Union’s sovereign-infrastructure model (the IRIS² constellation), and Ukraine’s own steps toward establishing Space Forces. bhowmick2026lunar.summary: Analyses lunar water resource rights, safety zones and India's regulatory concerns.
bhowmick2026lunar.abstract: The Moon is becoming a realistic site for scientific missions, permanent research facilities, and commercial activity. One resource has become especially important: water ice near the lunar south pole. Lunar water is extremely valuable for future commercial space operations. Yet international space law does not clearly answer who may extract it, own it after extraction, exclude others from a working area, or resolve conflicts between competing missions. This paper examines the legal gap between the non-appropriation rule in Article II of the Outer Space Treaty 1967 and the growing practice of commercial space-resource extraction. It argues that the most difficult issue is not simply whether a company can own extracted lunar water. The harder issue is whether “safety zones” around lunar operations may become de facto exclusive areas, allowing powerful States and companies to control the most useful sites without formally claiming sovereignty. The Artemis Accords support resource extraction and coordination zones, while the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space is developing non-binding principles on space-resource activities. India’s Space Policy 2023 also allows non-government entities to commercially recover, possess, own, transport, use, and sell space resources. bhambhani2026technological.summary: Reviews literature and runs a simplified Python scenario model of feedstock throughput and resource variables to assess commercial viability of asteroid resource extraction.
bhambhani2026technological.abstract: This independent research project investigates the technological and economic constraints affecting the commercial viability of asteroid-resource extraction. The study combines a review of NASA publications and peer-reviewed scientific literature with a simplified Python-based computational scenario model. The model examines how variables including feedstock throughput, resource concentration, extraction efficiency, delivery efficiency, fixed development costs and operating expenses influence the break-even price of delivered asteroid resources. Sensitivity analyses are conducted to examine how changes in the model's baseline assumptions affect the resulting economic estimates. The findings highlight the importance of resource accessibility, extraction performance, infrastructure costs and transportation when evaluating potential asteroid-mining operations. The numerical assumptions used in the computational model are illustrative and should not be interpreted as predictions or commercial estimates for an actual asteroid-mining mission. The record includes the research paper, Python source code, figures, model inputs and output files to support reproducibility. This work has not undergone formal academic peer review.

adebayo2026equity.summary: Rethinks the role of developing nations in equity and international space law governance.
adebayo2026equity.abstract: The governance of outer space is anchored in the principles of peaceful use, non-appropriation, and the "province of all mankind," as codified in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST).The rapid commercialization of space activities and the dominance of technologically advanced states have exposed significant inequities within the current international legal regime.This article examines the concept of equity in outer space governance, explicitly reconceptualizing the role of developing nations in the formulation and application of international space law.Utilizing doctrinal legal analysis, the study argues that while the OST establishes formal legal equality, structural disparities in technological capacity, orbital access, and norm-setting authority undermine substantive equity.Furthermore, the article critiques emerging unilateral and bilateral frameworks, such as national space resource legislation and the Artemis Accords, for their potential to erode multilateralism and inclusivity.The study contends that international cooperation must be operationalized not merely as an aspiration, but as a mechanism for capacity building and technology transfer.It concludes that achieving true equity requires a shift from aspirational principles to practical, establish International Outer Space Authority, binding legal and institutional tools that guarantee the substantive participation of developing nations in preserving outer space as an intergenerational resource.

simmonds2026space.summary: Examines legal implications of communications latency and time dilation in deep space missions.
simmonds2026space.abstract: Abstract The Artemis II and IV missions mark the first visit to the moon for human beings for over 50 years. During their voyage, the astronauts will experience time-lags in their communications with Earth owing to the inherent limitations of radio communication: nothing, not even radio waves, can travel faster than the speed of light. Should humanity venture into ‘deep space’, the time lag will increase in proportion to the distance travelled from Earth, moving from a few seconds to many minutes. This brings significant challenges for law and legal processes. If human beings travel as far as Mars, the disconnect could be anywhere up to 24 min at the furthest distance. Cross-examination or the deployment of leading questions becomes ineffective as an investigatory technique between parties on Earth and parties in deep space. Questions arise as to the commencement dates of statutes, whether they commence at the same time on Earth as they do by the frame of reference of a deep space crew. Routine contractual matters such as offer and acceptance also become uncertain between parties on Earth and those in deep space. Should human beings develop the technology to travel close to the speed of light, not only will these problems still be evident, they will also be compounded by the phenomenon of ‘time dilation’. As matters involving communication and symbols, what extent can these problems be examined through legal semiotics?

webukha2025assessing.summary: Assesses influence of Kenya's space programme on its foreign policy.
webukha2025assessing.abstract: The USA, Russia, and China have historically dominated the space race, with the African continent recently venturing into it. Kenya formed its own Kenya Space Agency to spearhead the process. This study investigated the influence of Kenya’s space exploration on its foreign policy dynamics with the United States. The objective was to evaluate challenges and opportunities of Kenya-USA relations in space exploration in regard to foreign policy. The research adopted a correlational method of study to examine relationships between the countries, borrowing from systems theory and grounded theory. The study adopted a stratified random sampling method. It involved stratifying the population, defining a number of separate partitions using sample size, and combining the results to obtain the required stratified sample. By ensuring that each stratum is represented in the sample, stratified sampling helped to ensure that the sample reflects the diversity of the population. A sample of 100 respondents was drawn from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; 50 were space experts and 50 were diplomats drawn from the two countries. tan2025biomimicry.summary: Thesis developing bio-inspired swarm robotics and nature-inspired methods to automate mining, including off-Earth.
tan2025biomimicry.abstract: This thesis introduces new methods for automating mining both on-Earth and off-Earth through bio-inspired decentralised swarm robotics and other nature-inspired methods and designs. As mining expands into harsher, more dangerous, and environmentally complex frontiers, e.g. deep underground workings, vast open pit mines, remnant ore extractions on Earth, and to off-Earth mining on Mars, the Moon and asteroids, the traditional centralized machines would struggle to adapt to these new conditions. For these, new swarm robotics models have been proposed that draw on the collective behaviours of leaf-cutter ants, honeybees, and fireflies to coordinate decentralized small autonomous agents via discrete state machines and peer-to-peer fault-tolerant signalling. By combining theoretical frameworks, an artificial bee colony optimization (ABCO) algorithm has been developed and tested in Matlab Simulink environment allowing to achieve collision avoidance, optimizing robot numbers for maximum performance and reducing the convergence time. Four new swarm robotic models have been proposed: baseline, ant, firefly, and honeybee models, to achieve reduction in energy consumption, ore delivery time and haul distance travelled for more efficient mining practices. These new nature-inspired algorithms have been developed for further optimizing resource exploration, precision mining, and ore logistics. They have been tested in complex Gazebo and ROS simulation environments for efficiency evaluation

khan2025cyber.summary: Argues for cybersecurity and cyber wargaming in the space domain for national security.
khan2025cyber.abstract: In the nascent era of outer space exploration and advancing technologies, this undertaking underscores that the need for cybersecurity in the space domain is a cornerstone for developing and maintaining a secure cyber environment during the entire lifecycle of space missions. It takes a relentless commitment: the complex coupling of disparate pieces of government, civil society, arms, and business into a single full-cycle operation. Cyber-attacks on space infrastructure such as malware installation, ransomware attack, and data/system hacking breaches are serious threats. The areas that are more susceptible to such attacks are revealed in this research, e.g., telecommunications, supply chain, national security, IoT/internet access, and global economies of scale. This project outlines primary goals, first by providing stakeholders insight into the state of play of current cyber wargaming, identifying trends, and closing with a sound framework for the integration of cyber and space-domain environments where impacts will be considerable. The integrated assessment involves technical and non-technical methods of strategic planning and emphasizes cooperation between public and private organizations. pietrzak2025economic.summary: Applies a modified structure-conduct-performance framework to space sector development amid satellite growth and geopolitical tension.
pietrzak2025economic.abstract: Background: The global space economy has grown remarkably, witnessing a 10-fold increase in active satellites during the last 15 years. This growth was accompanied by both the increase in geopolitical tensions feeding huge investments (the New Space Race), on the one hand, and the transformation, shifting from a domain historically dominated by government-led programs to one partially energized by commercial players and innovative business models (“New Space”), on the other hand. Objective: To assess the space economy’s current state and future prospects by considering its economic and social dimensions. Methods: Over 120 scholarly articles and “grey” literature positions (e.g., industry reports) were reviewed. The review was structured by a modified Structure–Conduct–Performance framework originally developed by industrial organization (IO) scholars. Findings: Outer space creates extremely harsh conditions for placing and operating objects in orbits, which results in high launching costs, steep reliability standards, capital intensity, and risks that are unmatched in most terrestrial industries. One of the main motivations to venture into this harsh domain was, and still is, the desire to dominate or the fear of being subjugated by others. poirier2025establishing.summary: Explores governance of cyber operations by space and cyber commands.
poirier2025establishing.abstract: During the past decade, major spacefaring nations have updated their space governance, establishing space forces and space commands now designed to address the evolving threat landscape in outer space. In parallel, the threat landscape has also evolved in cyberspace with a skyrocketing number of attacks coming from an increasingly diversified pool of actors, requiring governance changes authorizing the establishment of cyber forces and cyber commands. Both space and cyberspace are now increasingly recognized as warfighting domains and armed forces are conducting, or training to conduct, cyber-enabled space operations, which remain a new set of operations for which governance, operational modes, processes, and doctrines have to be adopted. The paper will aim at providing an overview of the governance of cyber-enabled operations in space and cyber commands and the challenges that these new missions face from the organizational perspective. First, the paper will provide case studies on the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, and France, looking particularly into the governance, mandates and responsibilities regarding cyber operations. Then, the paper will analyze challenges and shortcomings associated with the establishment of responsibilities for cyber operations in Space and Cyber Commands.
